Whereas advanced monitoring in the 1980s only required a few dissolved oxygen sensors, it is now typical to find sensors for a wide range of physico-chemical variables at facilities; for example, dissolved oxygen, oxidation-reduction potential, pH, temperature, total suspended solids, chemical oxygen demand (COD), and analyzers or ion-selective sensors for nitrogen and ortho-phosphate nutrients. This investment has led to a rich stream of data. A typical WRRF collects as many as 30,000 simultaneous signals. The potential of this data stream is rarely exploited today due to challenges with sensor management, data quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC), and a historical lack of drivers to extract valuable information from such data. Today, the potential power of the information contained in these data is extraordinary and can ensure the efficient and reliable application of novel, highly efficient WRRF processes, given that their state is sensitive to disturbances and is only optimal in a narrow region of operation. Advancements in technologies for data-driven analytics, diagnostics, and control from the field of ML can now be deployed at scale on premise or in the cloud. Recent advancements in computing hardware (e.g., graphics processing unit (GPU) computing) and algorithms (e.g., deep learning) vastly accelerated AI model experiments and development. In contrast to mechanistic modeling, ML offers the promise of highly automated systems that produce insights and recommendations for optimal operation. The combination of state-of-the-art sensor signals with ML methods will enable optimal operation of the selected high-efficiency processes in the face of disturbing events and upsets. This project integrates recent advancements in next generation sensors and ML tools to achieve full-scale process efficiencies while better achieving treatment goals (e.g., reduce energy and chemical inputs, maximize energy and nutrient recovery). In addition to developing and demonstrating data-driven process controls in real full-scale facilities for five Applications, this project created an industry-wide accessible ML Toolkit to help others more broadly integrate innovations in sensing and data-driven process control to improve WRRF performance. 1.4 ML Toolkit The water sector may have all the best sensors, tools, and technology available to implement ML, but without people, namely professionals trained in ML related disciplines, new ML approaches will not be able to be implemented. The water sector is currently lagging behind 6 The Water Research Foundation other sectors in terms of adoption of ML and AI, and workforce is one of the key challenges. The water sector needs to consider how to attract more computer scientists, data scientists, statisticians, etc. Additionally, the water sector can train wastewater process engineers in ML related disciplines. The ML Toolkit was designed to specifically help support the professional growth, development, and training of wastewater process engineers and others new to the realm of ML and artificial intelligence (AI) to enable more broad-scale implementation of these solutions.
